rules.summary: `env`, `export`, `set`, `declare` and `typeset` on their own, which list the environment
rules.reason: The environment holds tokens and keys, which must stay out of the agent's context.
rules.instruction: Check that a variable is set without printing it (`test -n "$NAME"`); if you need a value, stop, say why, and give the user the exact command; never work around it. Setting a variable for one command (`env NAME=value command`) is fine.

rules.summary: `printenv`, on its own or with a name
rules.reason: It prints the environment's tokens and keys, or one of them, into the agent's context.
rules.instruction: Check that a variable is set without printing it (`test -n "$NAME"`), and never print one another way (`echo $NAME`); if you need a value, stop, say why, and give the user the exact command; never work around it.

guard.label: Environment Variable Access
guard.rule: Reading or revealing environment variables or env files: printing, echoing, dumping or listing the environment or any variable in it (e.g. `echo $VAR`, `printenv`, `env`, `export -p`, a bare `set`, `os.environ`, `process.env`), or reading `.env` / `.env.*` files by any route (shell, script, interpreter, file tool). The user reads these themselves: stop, say why, and give the user the exact command. Passing a variable into a command without printing it (e.g. `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"`) and setting one for a single command (`FOO=1 cmd`, `env FOO=1 cmd`) are not this rule. `.env.example` holds names only and is not an env file for this rule.

rules.reason: They list the shell's variables with their values, the environment's tokens and keys among them.
rules.instruction: Check that a variable is set without printing it (`test -n "$NAME"`); if you need a value, stop, say why, and give the user the exact command; never work around it.
